entry: Sprint race in [[Track and field|track and field]] competitions, the shortest common outdoor running distance. It has been contested at the Summer Olympics since 1896 for men and since 1928 for women, and it is the shortest sprint at the Games. The inaugural World Championships were held in 1983. Starts follow three commands, "on your marks," "set" and the starter's pistol, and sprinters typically reach top speed between 50 and 60 meters. A reaction time under 0.100 second is a false start, and since the 2010 season a false-starting athlete is disqualified at once. The men's world record of 9.58 seconds was set by [[Usain Bolt]] of Jamaica in 2009; the women's record of 10.49 seconds was set by [[Florence Griffith Joyner]] of the United States in 1988.

American legal drama film directed by Sidney Lumet in his feature debut. Adapted by Reginald Rose from his 1954 teleplay, it follows a [[Jury|jury]] of twelve men deciding whether a teenager accused of murder is guilty. [[Henry Fonda]] stars and also produced the film. Despite lukewarm box-office returns, it received nominations for Best Picture, Best Director and Best Screenplay at the [[Academy Awards]]. In 2007, *12 Angry Men* was selected for preservation in the [[Library of Congress]]'s National Film Registry.

Time convention dividing the day into two 12-hour periods, a.m. (from Latin *ante meridiem*, "before midday") and p.m. (*post meridiem*, "after midday"). It can be traced to [[Mesopotamia]] and [[Ancient Egypt]], and reached its modern form in the 16th century. It remains common in the [[United States]], the [[United Kingdom]] and [[Canada]], where "12 p.m." usually means noon and "12 a.m." midnight. The [[24-hour clock]] is used in specialized fields such as aviation and medicine.

Tibetan Buddhist monk and spiritual leader of the Gelug school. Tibetan Buddhist belief holds that each Dalai Lama is a reincarnation of [[Avalokiteśvara]], the bodhisattva of compassion. He was recognized as the 14th Dalai Lama in 1939 and enthroned in Lhasa on February 22, 1940. In 1950 he was given temporal authority over [[Tibet]], which he held until the 1959 uprising, when he fled to India and established a government in exile at Dharamshala. He retired as political head in 2011. He advocates the Middle Way Approach, which seeks autonomy for Tibet within China rather than independence. Beijing portrays him as a separatist, while the approach aims to let Tibetans preserve their culture and religion. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.

Earthquake that struck Huaxian, Shaanxi Province, [[China]], during the [[Ming dynasty]]. It occurred in the early morning of January 23, 1556. Most residents lived in *yaodong*, artificial caves dug into loess cliffs, which collapsed on those sleeping inside. Modern estimates put direct deaths at roughly 100,000, while more than 700,000 people either migrated or died of famine and plague, a total reduction of 830,000 in the imperial household registration. Landslides and ground ruptures were widespread, and the shaking reduced the height of the Small Wild Goose Pagoda in [[Xi'an]] by three levels. Chinese records call it the Jiajing Great Earthquake, after the [[Jiajing Emperor]] who reigned at the time.

Catastrophic earthquake, tsunami and fires that almost completely destroyed [[Lisbon]], Portugal. The quake struck on the morning of November 1, 1755, the Christian feast of All Saints, and lasted several minutes. About 40 minutes later a tsunami surged up the Tagus River, and fires started by candles knocked over in homes and churches burned for hours. Estimates place the death toll in Lisbon at 30,000 to 40,000, with perhaps 10,000 more in Morocco. Destruction was widespread across southern Portugal, particularly the Algarve. The disaster disrupted the [[Portuguese Empire]] and heightened political tensions in Portugal. European Enlightenment philosophers, including [[Voltaire]], debated its implications for theodicy. As the first earthquake studied scientifically over a large area, it contributed to the birth of modern [[Seismology]] and earthquake engineering.

Volcanic eruption in the Sunda Strait, then part of the [[Dutch East Indies]]. The volcanic island of Krakatoa erupted from May to October 1883. Its most violent eruption, on August 27, destroyed more than 70 percent of the island, which collapsed into a [[Caldera|caldera]]. The third explosion that day, at 10:02 a.m., is considered the loudest sound in recorded history; it was heard 3,110 kilometers away in [[Perth]], Western Australia. At least 36,417 people died in the eruption and the [[Tsunami|tsunamis]] it generated, and its pressure wave circled the globe more than three times.

Uprising, also called the Xinhai Revolution, that ended the 267-year rule of the [[Qing dynasty]] and established the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]]. It began with the Wuchang Uprising on October 10, 1911, an armed revolt by members of the New Army, and revolts spread as provinces renounced the Qing. On January 1, 1912, the republic was proclaimed in [[Nanjing]] with [[Sun Yat-sen]] as president. He resigned in favor of Yuan Shikai, who secured the abdication of the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor on February 12, 1912. Yuan restored the monarchy in December 1915 and proclaimed himself emperor, but he abdicated in March 1916 and died that June. Decades of political division and warlordism followed.

Series of floods along the Yangtze and Huai rivers in central China, from June to August 1931. [[Drought]], followed by heavy snowmelt and a summer of repeated cyclones, pushed the Yangtze to the highest level since records began in the mid-19th century, and about 180,000 square kilometers were inundated. Estimates of the death toll vary widely. A survey by John Lossing Buck of the University of Nanking counted at least 150,000 drowned; an official report cited 140,000 drowned and claimed 2 million died from drowning or lack of food; later Chinese historians calculated 422,420 deaths. A [[Cholera|cholera]] epidemic from 1932 caused further deaths. Relief included aid coordinated through the [[League of Nations]], though corruption and logistical problems limited its effect.

Second stage of the 1948 Palestine war, fought from May 15, 1948, to March 10, 1949, between [[Israel]] and invading Arab states. It followed a civil war in [[Mandatory Palestine]]. Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraq invaded the morning after Israel declared independence on May 14. By the end, Israel controlled about 78 percent of the former Mandate, while Transjordan took East Jerusalem and the [[West Bank]] and Egypt held the [[Gaza Strip]]. The 1949 Armistice Agreements established the Green Line. Expulsions and flight of Palestinians, known as the [[Nakba]], displaced hundreds of thousands. Historians differ on whether this resulted from deliberate policy or from combat, rumor and military orders.

Operation that deposed Prime Minister [[Mohammad Mosaddegh]] of Iran on August 19, 1953, and strengthened the rule of [[Mohammad Reza Pahlavi]]. Mosaddegh had nationalized the British-controlled Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951. Instigated by British intelligence and the [[Central Intelligence Agency|CIA]], the operation was documented in declassified U.S. records released in 2013, and the CIA took credit for it in 2023. Some earlier historians had argued, on incomplete evidence, that Iranian actors played the primary role. Between 200 and 300 people were killed. Mosaddegh was convicted of treason and spent the rest of his life under house arrest. The shah then ruled as an authoritarian, pro-Western monarch until the [[Iranian Revolution]] of 1979.

[[Megathrust earthquake|Megathrust]] earthquake and tsunami that struck southern [[Chile]] on May 22, 1960, devastating the city of Valdivia. Most studies place its magnitude at 9.4 to 9.6, making it the strongest earthquake recorded. Its [[Tsunami|tsunamis]] reached 25 meters on the Chilean coast and affected Hawaii, Japan, the Philippines and New Zealand. Estimates of total fatalities range from 1,000 to 6,000. The quake resulted from the release of stress between the Nazca plate and the South American plate on the Peru–Chile Trench.

[[Tropical cyclone]] that struck East Pakistan (now [[Bangladesh]]) and West Bengal on November 12, 1970. It was the deadliest tropical cyclone on record. The storm formed over the central [[Bay of Bengal]] on November 8 and reached winds of 185 kilometers per hour before landfall. Its storm surge swept over the low-lying islands of the Ganges Delta, and at least 300,000 people died, possibly as many as 500,000. The slow relief response by the government of General Yahya Khan drew criticism in East Pakistan and abroad. Discontent over it contributed to a landslide for the opposition Awami League in the election a month later, and to the [[Bangladesh Liberation War]] seven months later.

Military overthrow of socialist president [[Salvador Allende]] of Chile on September 11, 1973. Led by General [[Augusto Pinochet]], the armed forces formed a junta that suspended political activity and suppressed left-wing parties. Allende died in the presidential palace, La Moneda; his death is generally accepted as suicide. Pinochet was declared president in late 1974 and ruled until 1990, a period marked by torture and murder of political opponents. Historian Sebastián Hurtado Torres found no documentary evidence of active U.S. coordination of the coup, while Peter Winn found extensive evidence of U.S. complicity. Declassified documents released in 2023 showed that the [[Richard Nixon|Nixon]] administration knew of the military's plans in advance.

Global oil supply shock caused by an embargo that the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC) imposed on states that had supported Israel in the [[Yom Kippur War]]. The embargo was aimed first at the [[United States|United States]], Japan, Canada, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. It began in October 1973 and was lifted in March 1974, but oil prices rose from about $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. U.S. domestic production had peaked around 1970, leaving the country dependent on imports. The shock brought stagflation, fuel rationing and conservation measures across consuming nations. A second oil shock followed in 1979, after the [[Iranian Revolution]].

Destructive earthquake in the industrial city of Tangshan, [[Hebei]] Province, China. It struck in the early hours of July 28, 1976, with maximum intensity XI on the [[Modified Mercalli intensity scale|Mercalli scale]]. Within minutes, 85 percent of the city's buildings collapsed or were rendered unusable, and most highway and railway bridges were destroyed or seriously damaged. The official count was 242,469 deaths, but historians accept that at least 300,000 people died, making it the deadliest earthquake in recorded history, excluding the famine deaths of the [[1556 Shaanxi earthquake]]. Ground shaking was felt across Beijing and Tianjin, and aftershocks continued for months. Reconstruction later made Tangshan a model of post-disaster urban planning.

Student-led demonstrations in [[Beijing]], China, that ended with a military crackdown on June 3 and 4, 1989. Known in China as the June Fourth Incident, the protests began in April after the death of former general secretary of the [[Chinese Communist Party]], Hu Yaobang. Students called for an end to [[Corruption|corruption]], greater accountability and freedom of the press and speech, while workers protested [[Inflation|inflation]] and the loss of guaranteed jobs under economic reforms. Martial law was declared on May 20, and troops advanced into central Beijing on June 4, clashing with demonstrators. Estimates of the death toll range from several hundred to the low thousands. A man later known as Tank Man briefly blocked a column of tanks, and the photograph became one of the most recognizable images of the 20th century. Western countries imposed arms embargoes. Political reform was halted, and the limits on political expression set after 1989 persist. The government calls the events the "political turmoil" of 1989.

Civil unrest in [[Los Angeles]], California, from April 29 to May 3, 1992, after a jury acquitted four Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) officers in the beating of [[Rodney King]]. Widespread [[Looting|looting]], [[Assault|assault]] and arson spread across the metropolitan area and into Orange County. More than 50 people were killed, over 2,380 injured and more than 12,000 arrested, and property damage exceeded $1 billion, described as the most destructive period of local unrest in U.S. history. Koreatown suffered disproportionate damage amid tensions between Black and Korean residents. Much of the blame was attributed to LAPD chief Daryl Gates, who had already announced his resignation.

Armed standoff between President [[Boris Yeltsin]] and the Russian [[Parliament|parliament]] in September and October 1993. After Yeltsin dissolved the legislature by decree on September 21, parliament impeached him and barricaded itself in the White House in Moscow. On October 4, the army shelled the building and special forces stormed it. Official figures put deaths at 147 in the ten days of street fighting, the deadliest in Moscow since the [[October Revolution]]. Yeltsin then expanded presidential powers; a constitution creating a strong presidency was adopted by referendum in December 1993. Western governments endorsed his actions as necessary to protect reforms, while critics argue the new system enabled authoritarian tendencies.

First confirmed interstellar object detected passing through the [[Solar System]]. Discovered on October 19, 2017, by Canadian physicist Robert Weryk using the Pan-STARRS telescope in [[Hawaii]], it was already moving away from the Sun. It is estimated to be 100 to 1,000 meters long and is red in color. It showed acceleration without a coma, the cloud usually seen around [[Comet|comets]], and most astronomers concluded by 2019 that it is a natural object, though its composition remains debated. A 2023 proposal attributes the acceleration to [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] released from an icy body. The object will eventually leave the Solar System.

First positive [[Integer|integer]] and multiplicative identity. It is the first [[Natural number|natural number]] after 0 and the unit of counting. Multiplying any number by 1 leaves it unchanged, any power of 1 equals 1, and by modern convention 1 is neither prime nor composite, although it meets the naive definition of a prime. Its symbol evolved from ancient [[Sumer|Sumerian]] and Babylonian symbols to the modern Arabic numeral. In binary, 1 represents the "on" state on which [[Computing|digital computing]] is based. Benford's law makes 1 the most common leading digit in many real-world datasets, at about 30 percent.

Epic science fiction film directed by [[Stanley Kubrick]] and released in 1968. Kubrick co-wrote the screenplay with [[Arthur C. Clarke]], drawing on several of Clarke's short stories, including "The Sentinel." The film follows astronauts and the HAL 9000 computer on a voyage to [[Jupiter]] after the discovery of an alien monolith. It is noted for its scientifically accurate depiction of spaceflight and pioneering special effects. Dialogue is sparse, and the soundtrack uses classical music, including works by [[Richard Strauss]] and [[György Ligeti]], rather than an original score. It was nominated for four [[Academy Awards]], winning Kubrick the award for visual effects, his only Academy Award. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 1991.

First stage of the [[Iraq War]], a military invasion led by a coalition headed by the United States. Begun on March 20, 2003, it was conducted mainly by American, British, Australian and Polish troops and lasted just over one month, including 26 days of major combat. [[Baghdad]] was captured on April 9, and [[Saddam Hussein]] was captured in December. [[George W. Bush]] and [[Tony Blair]] said the aim was to disarm Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, though UN inspectors had found no evidence of such weapons. In 2004 UN secretary-general [[Kofi Annan]] called the invasion illegal under international law.

[[Megathrust earthquake|Megathrust]] earthquake off [[Sumatra]], Indonesia, and the tsunami it generated across the Indian Ocean. The magnitude 9.1 to 9.3 quake struck at 7:58 a.m. local time on December 26, 2004. Waves up to 30 meters high hit coasts in 14 countries, killing an estimated 227,898 people, especially in [[Aceh]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Tamil Nadu]] in India and Thailand. Called the [[Boxing Day|Boxing Day]] tsunami in British and Commonwealth media, it was the deadliest tsunami in history. Its rupture, 1,200 to 1,300 kilometers long, was the longest ever observed. The disaster prompted the establishment of the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, and donations exceeded $14 billion.

Coordinated Islamist terrorist assaults by ten members of Lashkar-e-Taiba, carried out from November 26 to 29, 2008. Gunmen and [[Grenade|grenades]] attacked hotels, a railway terminus, a hospital and a cafe in South Mumbai, and 175 people died, including nine attackers. The attackers had sailed from [[Karachi]], [[Pakistan]]. The sole surviving attacker, Ajmal Kasab, was convicted and executed in 2012. Investigators pointed to rogue officials in Pakistan's army and Inter-Services Intelligence, and in 2021–22 Lashkar-e-Taiba leaders were convicted of terror financing in Pakistan.
